title: Teaching the Whole Person in the Age of AI
author: Jennifer W Shewmaker
summary: Shewmaker asks what a teacher is for when AI can explain, summarize and generate information in seconds, and answers that mission-driven higher education must be rooted in formation rather than information transfer. She rejects the view that professors simply profess while learning is the student's problem, invoking James K. A. Smith's critique of treating people as brains on sticks. Drawing on Parker Palmer's The Courage to Teach, she argues that good teaching flows from the teacher's identity and integrity, which requires showing up as a whole person, admitting ignorance and sharing mistakes. She highlights the Teaching Examen from Notre Dame's DELTA framework, which asks teachers whether their classrooms honor dignity, embodiment, love, transcendence and agency. Her own example is Lipscomb's first-year Compass Points gatherings, where everyone, faculty included, puts away personal technology to practice being fully present. She ends with two reflection questions on presence and modeling, and a note on how she used AI only for developmental feedback on her own draft.
points: Shewmaker argues AI makes the formation model of teaching more urgent because it can do much of the transmission work.
Following Palmer, she treats the humanity of teacher and student as essential to formation rather than an inefficiency to engineer away.
The DELTA Teaching Examen asks teachers to reflect on dignity, embodiment, love, transcendence and agency in their classrooms.
Her device-free Compass Points sessions are presented as a concrete way to practice embodied presence with students.
She models transparent AI use by explaining that she wrote the full draft herself before asking AI for editing feedback.
quotes: What is a teacher for when information is available everywhere and artificial intelligence can explain, summarize, and generate it in seconds? For mission-driven institutions of higher education, the answer cannot simply be delivering more information.

If education is primarily the transmission of information, increasingly powerful technologies can perform much of that work. But if education is the formation of people, the teacher’s presence, integrity, judgment, and care become more important than ever.
Approaching students as whole people requires us to show up as whole people too: to be vulnerable, to say, “I don’t know,” and to share some of our own mistakes.

Palmer challenges us to recognize that the humanity of both student and teacher is not an inconvenience to be engineered out of the educational experience. It is part of what makes formation possible.
In a culture where technology is pervasive, I believe we must explicitly name these practices, explain why they matter, and practice them alongside our students.
They need teachers who understand that education is not simply the transfer of knowledge, but the deeply human work of formation.
